title: Economic Report of the President 2026, Chapter 8: Strengthening the United States' Defense Industrial Base
date_evidence: Published at https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/ERP-2026-8.-Strengthening-the-United-States-Defense-Industrial-Base.pdf — the 2026 Economic Report of the President (uploads/2026/04/), Chapter 8.
key_claim: The defence industrial base's external uncertainty stems from demand being largely determined by the annual appropriations process, with limited multiyear procurement leaving many markets without a reliable signal of future demand, creating a hold-up problem that deters firms from investing in capacity; the policy answer is to increase the domestic demand signal through multiyear contracts and to crowd in private capital, including via the One Big Beautiful Bill Act expanding the Office of Strategic Capital to support up to $100 billion in loanable funds and the MP Materials package of a $150 million OSC loan plus $400 million in preferred equity; manufacturing was just 10 percent of GDP in 2024 down from 16 percent in 1997, and defense-related employment fell by 2.1 million between 1985 and 2021.
frame_summary: The Council of Economic Advisers argues the defence industrial base's core economic problem is monopsony-driven demand uncertainty and a hold-up problem, which the government should fix by stabilising the demand signal and crowding in private capital rather than by spending alone.
notes: Tier 1 canonical statement of the demand-signal / hold-up framing. Date from the 2026 ERP edition and the April 2026 upload path.

publisher: European Commission, Directorate-General for Defence Industry and Space
title: EDIP: Commission adopts EUR 1.5 billion work programme to boost European and Ukrainian defence industry
date_evidence: News article — 30 March 2026 — Directorate-General for Defence Industry and Space. 'Publication date: 30 March 2026'.
key_claim: The European Commission adopted a EUR 1.5 billion EDIP work programme, with more than EUR 700 million to support production increases of key defence products including counter-drone systems, missiles and ammunition, and EUR 240 million for joint procurement by Member States and Norway; EDIP builds on the EDIRPA common-procurement and ASAP ammunition-production regulations to give them a longer-term and more structured perspective, and introduces the Structure for European Armament Programme to aggregate demand.
frame_summary: The European Commission argues that pooling and aggregating European demand through EDIP, and funding production-capacity increases, is the way to convert higher spending into durable industrial capacity rather than mere price inflation.
notes: Tier 1 EU-side anchor for the demand-aggregation strand of the signal.

publisher: Center for Strategic and International Studies
title: Rebuilding U.S. Missile Inventory: A Multiyear Project
key_claim: CSIS finds that the problem today isn't money, it's time: production lead times for key munitions run 34 to 39 months, and replacing Tomahawk, THAAD and Patriot inventories will take three or more years, leaving a window of vulnerability; the Trump administration has signed framework agreements with industry to expand capacity over the next five to seven years, with Lockheed Martin planning to quadruple THAAD capacity and scale PAC-3 production toward a surge rate of 2,000 interceptors a year, but capacity does not equate to actual production.
frame_summary: CSIS argues that with funding now bipartisan and abundant, the binding constraint on rebuilding U.S. munitions stockpiles is time-to-capacity, and that framework agreements paying industry to expand are the central instrument for closing the gap.
verbatim_quote: the problem today isn't money; it's time
notes: Tier 2 anchor for the 'money is not the constraint' inversion and the framework-agreement instrument.

publisher: Center for Strategic and International Studies
title: Last Rounds? Status of Key Munitions at the Iran War Ceasefire
date_evidence: meta-citation_publication_date: Tue, 04/21/2026 - 12:00 ; 'Last Rounds? Status of Key Munitions at the Iran War Ceasefire'.
key_claim: CSIS assesses that the United States depleted its missile inventories during the 39-day bombing and air-defence campaign against Iran but retains enough for any plausible scenario in that war, with the real risk lying in a future war against a peer competitor such as China before stockpiles are rebuilt.
frame_summary: CSIS argues that the Iran war exposed how thin Western precision-munitions magazines are and created the political urgency now driving the munitions build-out.
notes: Tier 2 source for the demand-shock origin of the build-out.

title: The Pentagon wants a 188 percent bump for missile procurement. Can industry deliver?
key_claim: The FY2027 budget requests about $70.5 billion for missiles, a 188 percent increase over the $24.4 billion approved for FY2026, with roughly 55 percent sought through reconciliation so the money is available over a longer period; THAAD orders jump from 55 to 857 and the Tomahawk request is a 1,327 percent increase, and analyst Todd Harrison notes the approach is even better than multiyear procurement because the government can tell a contractor 'we already have the funding. We can now guarantee this to you', while solid rocket motors and seekers remain bottlenecks no dollar figure can quickly overcome.
frame_summary: Breaking Defense reports that the Pentagon's munitions plus-up is designed less to buy weapons this year than to send industry a multiyear, pre-funded demand guarantee large enough to justify capacity expansion.
verbatim_quote: we already have the funding. We can now guarantee this to you
notes: Tier 3, central to the demand-guarantee mechanism. Carries the $70.5bn, 188 percent, $24.4bn, 1,327 figures.

title: Billions are flowing into munitions, but there are limits to how quickly the U.S. can replenish its stockpiles
date_evidence: Terry Gerton — 'March 30, 2026 3:21 pm' — interview with Jerry McGinn, Director of the Center for the Industrial Base at CSIS.
key_claim: CSIS industrial-base director Jerry McGinn says the One Big Beautiful Bill Act put $25 billion into munitions and a roughly $200 billion supplemental is under discussion, and that companies respond to incentives, adjusting workforce and tooling to the demand signal from multiyear contracts; he cites the MP Materials deal as the template, a 10-year offtake agreement with a guaranteed price floor, a $150 million Office of Strategic Capital loan and up to $1 billion in private financing, with the government trying to create stability and demand to make the environment ripe for investment.
frame_summary: McGinn argues the government sets and regulates the defence market, so the decisive lever is the credibility and durability of its demand signal, not the headline budget number.
notes: Tier 3, carries the warm-base / demand-signal language and the $25bn, $200bn, $150m, $1bn, 10-year figures.

title: Pentagon requests more than $20B for strategic capital loan program in 2027
key_claim: The Defense Department is asking Congress for about $20.2 billion in FY2027 for the Defense Strategic Capital Credit Program run by the Office of Strategic Capital, more than an order of magnitude above the less than $1.5 billion allotted for FY2026, with the office offering direct loans of up to $150 million that can be combined with private equity and corporate debt to fully fund a project.
frame_summary: DefenseScoop reports that the Pentagon is scaling a government credit and loan-guarantee tool by more than tenfold, signalling a shift toward using the state's balance sheet to de-risk private capacity investment.
notes: Tier 3 for the OSC financing leg. Carries $20.2bn and less than $1.5bn.

title: The Primes Aren't the Real Bottleneck in U.S. Weapons Production
key_claim: Production timelines are set by thinly capitalised Tier-2 and Tier-3 suppliers, not the primes: the Department of Defense estimates it has lost more than 40 percent of its small business suppliers, 84 percent of primes have no visibility beyond their Tier-1 supplier, and unless multiyear contracts, loan guarantees and targeted government stock purchases reach the sub-tiers in a sustained and predictable way, increased spending will concentrate at the top of the pyramid while capacity constraints persist below.
frame_summary: Written by a defence-industry chief executive, the piece argues that demand guarantees aimed at prime contractors miss the real constraint, which is the financial fragility of the sub-tier supplier base.
notes: Tier 4 (author has disclosed commercial interest); used as the counter-argument and structural anchor (Jan 2026, 3-6m band, within 12 months).
